content:
The image shows large, white to silvery abnormal growths (galls) emerging from the corn plant at the ear/stalk region. The galls are bulbous, smooth, and covered with white tissue — they have not yet ruptured to release dark spore masses. The plant tissue around the galls still appears green and healthy.

This matches Common Smut perfectly: galls can appear on any above-ground part (ears, stalks, tassels, leaves), are initially covered with white to silvery tissue, and later develop dark masses of spores inside. The large, round, white galls in the image are classic early-stage Common Smut galls on the ear/stalk junction.

Head Smut was considered but ruled out: Head Smut replaces the entire ear/tassel and plants are typically dwarfed, whereas here the galls are discrete, localized abnormal growths on an otherwise healthy-looking plant.
